 National retail sales are projected to top $1 trillion during the 2026 holiday season, but surveys show consumers remain concerned about affordability and plan to seek sales, compare prices and manage their gift budgets.
 Metro Creative 
 CLARKSBURG, W.Va. — Americans are expected to spend more during the holiday shopping season this year, with national retail sales projected to top $1 trillion, even as consumers look for ways to stretch their budgets and manage rising costs.
 The National Retail Federation forecasts that U.S. retail sales in November and December will reach $1.013 trillion, a 4.2% increase over 2025, when holiday sales totaled $972 billion. The trade association released its forecast Oct. 15.
 Other forecasts also point to growth, although estimates vary depending on the period and types of spending measured.
 Deloitte projects holiday retail sales will total between $1.70 trillion and $1.71 trillion from November through January, an increase of 4% to 4.8% over the same period last year. The forecast includes a projected 7.5% to 8.4% increase in online holiday sales.
 However, expectations for higher overall sales do not necessarily mean individual shoppers plan to spend more on gifts.
 A survey released Oct. 20 by the National Retail Federation found that 56% of holiday shoppers expect the economy to affect their spending plans this year. Among those consumers, 43% said they planned to look for sales more often, 31% intended to compare prices online more frequently and 29% planned to use coupons more often.
 The survey, conducted by Prosper Insights & Analytics from Oct. 1-7, included 8,094 adult consumers and had a margin of error of plus or minus 1.1 percentage points.
 Consumers also are starting their shopping early in an effort to manage expenses. The survey found that 43% of holiday shoppers planned to begin browsing or buying before November, similar to the 42% who did so last year. Half of those shopping early said they wanted to spread out their holiday budgets, while 37% cited attractive prices and promotions.
 Still, many shoppers plan to wait for major sales events. Nearly two-thirds of consumers said they were likely to wait until Thanksgiving weekend to complete most of their holiday shopping.
 Other research suggests consumers may be trimming gift budgets even as overall retail sales increase.
 A NerdWallet survey released this fall found that Americans planning to purchase gifts expected to spend an average of $879, down 21% from $1,107 in 2025. The survey included more than 2,000 U.S. adults and also found that 92% planned to spend on holiday-related expenses, including gifts, travel and parties.
 Meanwhile, Deloitte's consumer survey found that households expected to spend an average of $1,654 on the holidays, up 4% from $1,595 in 2025. That estimate includes retail purchases and holiday activities, such as travel and entertainment.
 The differing estimates reflect variations in survey methods and the expenses included in each study.
 For retailers, the forecasts suggest consumers are still planning to celebrate the holidays but are paying close attention to value, promotions and where they spend their money.
 National Retail Federation President and CEO Matthew Shay said the organization expects consumers to prioritize the holiday season while remaining mindful of their budgets.
 Inflation, higher gasoline prices, interest rates and consumer debt remain concerns for retailers as they prepare for the season, according to the federation. It expects retailers to hire between 325,000 and 375,000 seasonal workers, roughly in line with last year's estimated 356,000 seasonal jobs.
 The National Retail Federation's forecast measures retail sales from Nov. 1 through Dec. 31 and excludes automobile dealers, gasoline stations and restaurants. Its projections are based on economic indicators including consumer spending, disposable personal income, employment, wages, inflation and previous monthly retail sales reports.
